instructions.name: close_shard
docs: Reclaim the rent a dormant shard is sitting on: closes its two ATAs and returns that
rent to the user. The USDC ATA's rent really is the user's own (`deposit_balance`,
`payer = authority`); the cbBTC ATA was created inside a Sat Rush claim CPI with the
shard PDA as payer — i.e. fronted by the crank-funded float — and returning it anyway is
deliberate policy: it is bounded, one-shot (~0.002 SOL), and not worth a second code
path. Refuses while the shard still holds anything, in its ATAs or in its Sat Rush
`Miner`.
**The shard's own SOL float is deliberately NOT swept.** The crank funds it so Sat Rush
has a rent payer for the ticket accounts it creates; paying it out would move protocol
money to the user, and since the crank re-funds on its next pass it would do so on a
loop. `WkShardClosed` therefore deliberately carries no lamport figure — see
`handle_close_shard`.
Leaves `Manager` and `Deployer` alive on purpose — they are what let the shard keep
signing, and a 1 BTC ticket cannot be proven absent on chain.

accounts.name: authority
docs: The user, and only the user. This destroys accounts, so unlike the claim paths it is
not open to a passer-by.

instructions.name: create_manager
docs: `index` lets one wallet hold several independent positions, one per operator it hires.
Pass 0 unless the user genuinely wants two operators running at once.

accounts.name: manager
docs: A PDA of the user's own key plus an index — not a keypair.
evore hands the user a keypair to keep safe; losing it strands the account. The index
recovers the one thing that keypair bought them: a wallet can hold several independent
positions, one per operator it hires. Most users only ever use index 0.

accounts.name: deployer
docs: A deposit is what GRANTS stake budget (`Deployer::stake_allowance`), so the account that
holds the budget has to be here.
Required, not optional: without it a deposit would be money the position is never
permitted to stake once `auto_reload` is false, which is a far more confusing failure
than needing settings saved first. `create_deployer` is already step one of onboarding
and the account is never closed, so the ordering costs nobody anything.

accounts.name: wk_auth
docs: only to own ATAs and to sign Sat Rush CPIs.

accounts.name: wk_auth_usd_ata
docs: Created on first deposit, so the user never has to think about it.

accounts.name: program
docs: This program's own program account. `init_config` is first-come-first-served on a
singleton PDA that can never be closed — without a gate, whoever landed it first in the
deploy-to-init window owned the config forever, and the only recovery was abandoning the
program id. The gate: the signer must be the program's UPGRADE AUTHORITY, proven by
walking program → ProgramData → upgrade_authority_address in `require_upgrade_authority`.

accounts.name: program_data
docs: the caller; the handler requires it to match the embedded address.

instructions.name: set_user_flags
docs: Move the user's own position switches — mining pause, vault-buy hold. See
`state::user_flag` for each bit and `SetUserFlags` for why this is its own instruction
rather than another `DeployerSettings` field.
Signed by the manager authority ONLY. An operator has no branch here by design.

instructions.name: withdraw_balance
docs: USDC only, mint checked against config. `amount = 0` withdraws everything.

instructions.name: withdraw_tokens
docs: Any mint — this is how cbBTC winnings leave. `amount = 0` withdraws everything.

instructions.name: wk_buy_epoch_tickets_batch
docs: Buy epoch tickets, counts named per shard by the crank. The knee/split policy that
used to live here is operator ticket policy now; the program enforces only the spend
(whole tickets, within SPENDABLE hashrate, operator-gated per user) and the page
mechanics. Order relative to the 1 BTC batch is the crank's own business.

accounts.name: crank
docs: Any operator's crank. De-gated globally, but every user in the batch is checked
against their own `deployer.deploy_authority` below — this instruction SPENDS the
user's hashrate, so it cannot be left open the way the claim paths are.

instructions.name: wk_buy_one_btc_tickets_batch
docs: Buy 1 BTC tickets, counts named per shard by the crank — same contract as the epoch
batch. Signature-bound: each user needs a fresh ticket keypair that signs.

accounts.name: crank
docs: Any operator's crank. De-gated globally, but every user in the batch is checked
against their own `deployer.deploy_authority` below — this instruction SPENDS the
user's hashrate, so it cannot be left open the way the claim paths are.

instructions.name: wk_claim_epoch_rewards_batch
docs: Collect epoch prizes. Win detection reads `winners[21]` on chain; a non-winner in the
batch is skipped rather than reverting the transaction.

accounts.name: crank
docs: Anyone may sign this. It only ever moves value TOWARD the user, so leaving it open is
a feature: a stalled or vanished operator can never strand someone's funds, and any
passer-by can help a user get paid.

instructions.name: wk_claim_one_btc_rewards_batch
docs: Collect the 1 BTC prize. One ticket account holds a block, so the win test is a range
check against `winningTicket`, not an equality.

accounts.name: crank
docs: Anyone may sign this. It only ever moves value TOWARD the user, so leaving it open is
a feature: a stalled or vanished operator can never strand someone's funds, and any
passer-by can help a user get paid.

accounts.name: satrush_config
docs: 2026-08-14 redeploy added this account to `claim_one_btc_reward`.

instructions.name: wk_claim_sats_batch
docs: Burn sats-vault shares to release locked hashrate, and take the cbBTC cash-back with it.
**How much to release is config, not an argument.** It reads
`param::CLAIM_SATS_TICKETS`, seeded at 0 = release everything. It was once a
caller-supplied `tickets_wanted`; nothing in production ever set it to anything but 0, so
it was a knob any signer could turn on a money path for no benefit. See that param for why
0 is the right value and not merely the convenient one.

accounts.name: crank
docs: Anyone may sign this. It only ever moves value TOWARD the user, so leaving it open is
a feature: a stalled or vanished operator can never strand someone's funds, and any
passer-by can help a user get paid.

accounts.name: token_mint
docs: RUSH mint, checked against Sat Rush's v2 config in the handler.

instructions.name: wk_claim_token_batch
docs: Burn each shard's Sat Rush v2 token-vault shares and collect the resulting RUSH plus
any cbBTC/hashrate released by the same claim. The wallet cannot call Sat Rush directly:
each Miner belongs to our `wk_auth` PDA, so this wrapper supplies the required signature.
Open to any payer because value only moves into user-controlled shards.

accounts.name: token_mint
docs: RUSH mint. Its address is checked against Sat Rush's v2 config in the handler.

instructions.name: wk_claim_usd_batch
docs: Pull USDC winnings back into each shard, where the next deploy spends them.
Runs for everyone owed something, UNCONDITIONALLY — `auto_reload` is deliberately not
consulted here, and since the thin-wrapper upgrade it is not consulted ANYWHERE on
chain: the reload preference is enforced by the crank's own ledger. Claiming and
staking are separate decisions: money the protocol owes a user must never be left
sitting in Sat Rush, whatever they asked their operator to do with it afterwards.

accounts.name: crank
docs: Anyone may sign this. It only ever moves value TOWARD the user, so leaving it open is
a feature: a stalled or vanished operator can never strand someone's funds, and any
passer-by can help a user get paid.

instructions.name: wk_close_one_btc_tickets_batch
docs: Reclaim the rent sitting in spent 1 BTC tickets. Sat Rush never does this for us — the
ticket owner must, and ours are PDAs only this program can sign for.
Refuses to run while the iteration is still `Open`, because a ticket closed before the
draw is an entry thrown away.

accounts.name: crank
docs: Anyone may sign. Rent flows to the shard that paid it, never to the caller, so an open
door costs nothing and means a vanished operator cannot strand a user's rent.

accounts.name: satrush_config
docs: 2026-08-14 redeploy added this account to `close_one_btc_ticket`.

instructions.name: wk_deploy_batch
docs: N items per call, each naming a shard, an amount, and a tile mask — THE CRANK CHOOSES
ALL THREE. This program is the bouncer, not the strategist: it checks each request
against the user's consent (fee ceilings, the `max_per_round` meter, wallet range),
the protocol's bounds (min/max amount, mask legality, divisibility), and the balance,
then charges our fee and CPIs Sat Rush's `deploy_public` with the request verbatim.
A request that fails a bound is SKIPPED (a `WkDeploySkipped` event), never resized,
and never reverts the batch because of one bad item.

accounts.name: crank
docs: **Any** operator's crank. Pays transaction fees and — since the thin-wrapper upgrade —
NAMES each item's amount and tile mask; what it cannot do is touch a user who did not
hire it, charge past their fee ceiling, or stake past their `max_per_round` meter.
Deliberately NOT constrained to `config.deploy_authority` — that global gate is what
made Whiteknight single-operator. The real security boundary is per user, below:
`deployer.deploy_authority == crank`.

accounts.name: operator_usd_ata
docs: Where the OPERATOR's fee lands — their own token account.
Safe to share across the batch: every user in it must already satisfy
`deployer.deploy_authority == crank`, so they all have the same operator. Constrained
to the signer, so a crank can only ever pay itself.

accounts.name: platform_usd_ata
docs: Where OUR platform cut lands. Checked against `config.fee_collector`, so no operator
can redirect it — this is the account that makes the platform self-enforcing rather
than a monthly invoice.

accounts.name: round
docs: compromised crank cannot point deploys at a stale or unrelated round.

instructions.name: wk_settle_batch
docs: Settle our own deployments — the ONLY way our shard PDAs can be credited hashrate.
**This instruction is open to any signer** (`WkSettleBatch::crank` carries no operator
check), because it only ever moves value toward the user.
What is NOT permissionless is Sat Rush's inner `settle_deploy_public`, which rejects any
signer that is not the deployment's own authority — corrected from the original plan
note, which had the crank calling them directly. Ours is a PDA, so the settle must route
through this program; but anyone at all may be the one to ask for it.

accounts.name: crank
docs: Anyone may sign this. It only ever moves value TOWARD the user, so leaving it open is
a feature: a stalled or vanished operator can never strand someone's funds, and any
passer-by can help a user get paid.

accounts.name: rent_recipient
docs: Where the closed deployment's rent goes. Must match the `SETTLE_RENT_TO_US` flag, so a
compromised crank cannot quietly redirect the refunds to itself when policy says the
user keeps them, or vice versa.

accounts.name: satrush_program
docs: as this same program id, so the outer instruction must grant it writable privilege.

types.name: BuyTicketItem
docs: One shard's ticket request, in WHOLE TICKETS — the unit both Sat Rush buy CPIs take on
the wire, so nothing is converted or floored between the crank's ask and the CPI. The
spend check is `units_for_tickets(tickets) <= Miner.hashrate_amount` (1 ticket = 100
units), exact and never partial: a request the bank cannot cover is skipped whole, so a
crank sizing bug surfaces as a skip event instead of a silent smaller buy.

fields.name: auth_id
docs: Shard index under the user's Manager; the item's remaining accounts must match it.

fields.name: tickets
docs: Whole tickets to buy for this shard. Zero is a skip (`ZeroRequest`), not an error.

types.name: ConfigKey
docs: Which named pubkey `SetKey` targets.

types.name: DeployItem
docs: One shard's deploy request, exactly as the crank chose it.
Borsh wire format: `auth_id u64 LE ‖ amount u64 LE ‖ tile_mask u32 LE` — 20 bytes per
item, length-prefixed as a vec. The instruction discriminator did not change with the
arg layout (Anchor sighash is name-only), so an OLD crank sending `Vec<u64>` against this
program fails borsh decode loudly rather than being misread — the intended atomic-cutover
failure mode.

fields.name: auth_id
docs: Shard index under the user's Manager; the item's five remaining accounts must match it.

fields.name: amount
docs: USDC micros THIS shard stakes this round — the bet, not including either fee leg,
both of which are charged on top exactly as before.

fields.name: tile_mask
docs: Bit i set ⇒ tile (i+1) selected. Forwarded to Sat Rush verbatim after `mask_is_legal`;
Sat Rush splits `amount` evenly across the set bits, which is why `amount` must divide
by the popcount (checked here, skipped if not — never rounded).

fields.name: deploy_authority
docs: **The operator this user has hired.** Set by the user, changeable by the user at any
time without moving funds or losing streak. Only this key may deploy for them.

fields.name: bps_fee
docs: What the operator actually charges. They set this themselves, and it is rejected at
deploy time if it exceeds the ceiling below.

fields.name: shard_count
docs: How many wallets the operator is running right now. Operator-writable, but only
within `max_shards`. Purely a wallet-count consent bound: the crank sizes each
wallet's stake itself, and the program's `auth_id < shard_count` check plus the
`max_per_round` meter are what bound the money.

fields.name: max_shards
docs: **The most wallets this user consents to being split across.** The operator picks the
actual `shard_count` above and may never exceed this - the same shape as the fee
ceilings, and for the same reason: more wallets cost the user more flat fee
(`param::PLATFORM_FLAT_FEE`, charged per wallet per round), so the ceiling is how they
bound that. 0 is read as 1.

fields.name: max_per_round
docs: **The most USDC this position may stake per round, TOTAL across every wallet.**
This is the thin-wrapper upgrade's load-bearing reinterpretation: the same byte slot
held `per_round_amount`, the EXACT bet the program divided across wallets. The crank
chooses each wallet's stake now, and this became the ceiling it must fit under —
enforced by the `last_round`/`staked_in_round` meter below as
`already_staked_this_round + this_amount <= max_per_round`, item skipped (never
clamped) on breach. Same offset, so every live account's "exact bet" became "cap at
that bet" at upgrade, which is the no-surprise migration: nobody can be staked MORE
than they were already staking until they raise it themselves.
0 is a legal value meaning "nothing may be staked" — the meter can never pass. There
is no settings-time bound against protocol params: the per-shard protocol cap
(`param::MAX_PER_ROUND_AMOUNT`) applies to each supplied amount at deploy time, where
it belongs; this field is a cross-shard TOTAL and the two are not comparable.

fields.name: tile_count
docs: ABANDONED — tile choice is supplied per deploy as `DeployItem.tile_mask`.

fields.name: run_rounds
docs: ABANDONED — session length is operator policy, counted in the crank's diary.

fields.name: when_funds_low
docs: ABANDONED — funds-low behavior (stop vs keep-running shrink) is crank sizing policy.

fields.name: max_per_tile
docs: ABANDONED — per-tile sizing is operator mask/amount policy.

fields.name: min_bet
docs: ABANDONED — minimum-bet preference is crank sizing policy (the PROTOCOL minimum,
`param::MIN_DEPLOY_AMOUNT`, is still enforced on every supplied amount).

fields.name: stop_level
docs: ABANDONED — the stop-level reserve is crank sizing policy.

fields.name: auto_reload
docs: ABANDONED — the winnings-recycling preference is operator policy backed by the
crank's own deposit/stake ledger. The old on-chain mechanism (`stake_allowance`
below) stopped being debited at the upgrade and cannot enforce it anymore.

fields.name: min_strike_pot_usd
docs: ABANDONED — the Sat Strike range (mine only while the pot is inside [min, max]) is
operator policy: the crank prices the pot off-chain and simply does not include a
gated shard in the batch. The on-chain valuation machinery this pair drove
(`strike_pot_usd`, the derived previous-round account) left with it.

fields.name: max_strike_pot_usd
docs: ABANDONED — the other end of the strike range; see `min_strike_pot_usd`.

fields.name: last_round
docs: The round `staked_in_round` refers to. A different `round_id` resets the meter.

fields.name: staked_in_round
docs: Staked so far this round, across every wallet. Compared against `max_per_round`
before every CPI; an item that would breach it is skipped, never clamped.

fields.name: rounds_played
docs: ABANDONED — rounds-deployed counter for the old on-chain `run_rounds` gate. Frozen at
its pre-upgrade value (`wk_deploy_batch` no longer increments it); session length is
counted in the crank's diary. Do not read it as current.

fields.name: stake_allowance
docs: ABANDONED as an enforcement mechanism — the lifetime stake budget that made
`auto_reload = false` mean something on chain. `wk_deploy_batch` no longer debits it,
so it can no longer bound anything; the reload preference is enforced by the crank's
own deposit/stake ledger. `deposit_balance` still CREDITS it (harmless, and it keeps
`WkDeposited.stake_allowance` meaning what it always meant), so the value reads as
"lifetime deposits minus pre-upgrade stakes" — history, not a budget.

fields.name: btc_share_bps
docs: ABANDONED — the user's fixed jackpot share of every ticket buy, in bps. The
epoch/1-BTC split is operator ticket policy now; the crank seeded this value into its
policy store at cutover. (Historically the first carve from the launch reserve, which
is why it sits after `bump`.)

fields.name: epoch_units_bought
docs: ABANDONED — the flow ledger that made the jackpot ratio a cumulative guarantee.
Frozen at its pre-upgrade value (the ticket handlers no longer write it).

fields.name: btc_units_bought
docs: ABANDONED — the other half of the frozen flow ledger.

fields.name: user_flags
docs: **The user's own switches** — see the `user_flag` module for each bit's exact meaning
(and which bits the program still reads). Written ONLY by `set_user_flags`, which is
gated on the manager authority, so an operator can never move a user's switches.
The fourth carve from the launch reserve, and the first one that is deliberately a bit
field rather than a named field: switches added here later cost enforcement code and
nothing else, where a named `bool` would change `DeployerSettings` and with it the wire
format of `create_deployer` and `update_deployer` — every live client, every time.

fields.name: reserved
docs: **Post-mainnet expansion room, and the reversal of an earlier decision.** The previous
stance — no spare bytes, rent is forever — was argued explicitly from "nothing is
deployed, so there is nothing to migrate". Deploying flips that argument on its head:
after launch, adding ANY user setting without this block changes `LEN`, and `LEN` is the
crank's `getProgramAccounts` `dataSize` filter — every existing user would vanish from
discovery until a migration touched every live account. With the block, a new field is a
carve-out from its front: `LEN` never moves, the filter never breaks, old accounts keep
decoding (their carved bytes read as zero, which every field here treats as "unset").
256 bytes costs each user ~0.0018 SOL (~$0.13 at $75) of rent, once. Two settings were
added in the week before launch alone (the strike range) — that is the growth rate this
insures against.

types.name: DeployerSettings
docs: Everything set when a position is created, in one struct so `create` and `update` cannot
drift apart.
Note this carries BOTH the operator's fee and the user's ceiling. At creation the user
signs for all of it — a frontend pre-fills the fee with its operator's published rate, and
the user is consenting to both the rate and the cap in one action. Afterwards the two are
controlled by different keys (see `handle_update_deployer`).

fields.name: deploy_authority
docs: Which operator to hire. Any key may be an operator; there is no registry.

fields.name: bps_fee
docs: What that operator charges. Must not exceed the ceiling below.

fields.name: expected_bps_fee
docs: The user's ceiling. 0 means "no ceiling" — only sensible when you ARE the operator.

fields.name: per_round_amount
docs: **Lands in `Deployer.max_per_round`**: the most USDC this position may stake per
round, TOTAL across every wallet. The wire field keeps its historical name so every
live client's create/update keeps decoding byte-for-byte — the recorded onboarding
transactions replayed in test_deploy_batch.rs are the proof that matters.

fields.name: shard_count
docs: How many wallets to run. Bounded by `max_shards` and the 21-wallet hard cap only.

fields.name: max_shards
docs: The most wallets this user consents to. The operator may move `shard_count` under it
and never above. 0 is read as 1.

fields.name: authority
docs: **Who controls the position now.** Mutable — `transfer_manager` moves it.

fields.name: seed_authority
docs: **The wallet the PDA was derived from, forever.** Set once at creation and never
written again.
This exists because the seed and the controller cannot be the same field. The address is
`["wk-manager", seed_authority, index]`, so if `transfer_manager` moved the value the
address is derived from, the account would stop re-deriving to itself: the new owner
fails `ConstraintSeeds`, the old owner fails `has_one`, and `resolve_user` fails
`BadPda` — locking BOTH parties out of a shard that still holds their money, with no
instruction able to reach it. Pinned by `after_a_transfer_the_new_owner_can_still_withdraw`.

fields.name: index
docs: Which of this wallet's positions this is. Stored as well as seeded, because
`resolve_user` has to re-derive the PDA from the account alone.

fields.name: reserved
docs: Post-mainnet expansion room — carve fields from the front so `LEN` never moves. Costs
each user ~0.0018 SOL of rent once; buys adding a field without migrating every live
Manager. See `Deployer::LEN` for the full argument.

types.name: WkAdminAccepted
docs: Step 2 — the handover completed and the old key is powerless from this slot on.

types.name: WkAdminTransferStarted
docs: Step 1 of the admin handover. Nothing changes until the pending key accepts.

fields.name: kind
docs: `CLAIM_USD` or `CLAIM_SATS`.

fields.name: amount
docs: USDC micros for a USD claim; shares burned for a sats claim.

fields.name: released_hashrate
docs: Hashrate units freed. Always 0 for `CLAIM_USD` — measured: it does not touch the lock.

fields.name: usd_amount
docs: MEASURED across the CPI. `amount` above is what we ASKED for (USDC owed, or shares to
burn); these two are what actually arrived in the shard. For a sats claim the difference
matters most: `amount` is shares burned, which is not a quantity of bitcoin, so without
`btc_amount` nothing on chain recorded how many satoshis the cash-back actually paid.

types.name: WkCollectSkipped
docs: One user was passed over during a collection batch, and this is why.
Emitted for EVERY pass-over, including the routine ones. That is deliberate and it is the
whole point: an operator reconciling "why has this shard not been paid" needs to see the
difference between *we looked and there was nothing there* and *we never looked at all*.
Absence of an event now means the shard was never in a batch, which is itself a finding.

fields.name: op
docs: One of the `OP_*` constants above.

fields.name: reason
docs: A `SkipCause` discriminant.

fields.name: fault
docs: `reason >= FIRST_FAULT`. Denormalised on purpose — an indexer filtering for "things that
need a human" must not have to know the numbering to do it.

fields.name: pending_admin
docs: Two-step handover so we cannot brick ourselves by setting a dead key.

fields.name: satrush_program
docs: NOT a const — lets us retarget devnet or a Sat Rush redeploy without an upgrade.

fields.name: reserved
docs: **Post-mainnet expansion room.** `params` (15 free u64 slots) and `flags` (60 free bits)
absorb every future NUMBER and SWITCH without an upgrade — but not a future named
pubkey (a second treasury, a new mint, a registry). This block absorbs that: carve a
field from its front, and `LEN` — which both off-chain readers length-check — never
moves. A singleton pays the extra rent exactly once, so unlike the per-user accounts
this trade was never close.

types.name: WkConfigInitialized
docs: The config singleton was born. One-time; every later change has its own event below.

types.name: WkDeploySkipped
docs: `reason` is a `SkipReason`. The crank must distinguish "the user asked to stop"
(`RunFinished`) from "the user is out of money" (`InsufficientFunds`) from "our config
no longer permits their settings" (`BadSettings`) — only the last is our problem to fix.

fields.name: fee
docs: The operator's cut.

fields.name: platform_fee
docs: Our platform cut. Emitting both separately is what lets an operator reconcile their
own revenue from chain without trusting our accounting — and lets us do the same.

fields.name: operator
docs: Which operator deployed this. On a multi-operator platform, "who did this" is no
longer implied by the program itself.

types.name: WkDeployerConfigured
docs: Emitted on every settings write, so what a round will actually cost is on chain and
indexable rather than only in a UI the user may not have read.
The reason this exists: **the flat fee legs are charged PER WALLET PER ROUND.** A user who
moves from 1 wallet to 3 pays the flat fee three times a round, and that is the single most
surprising thing about our pricing. `flat_fee_total` is the multiplied-out number, not the
per-wallet rate, precisely so nobody has to do the multiplication themselves to notice.

fields.name: deploy_authority
docs: **The operator this position hired** — the platform's central act, and previously the
one thing no event recorded: from events alone, a user firing an operator (whose deploys
then stop with `FeeAboveCeiling` skips) was indistinguishable from one replacing them.
Every settings write now names the operator in force after it.

fields.name: per_round_amount
docs: TOTAL staked per round, across all wallets.

fields.name: max_shards
docs: The ceiling the user consented to.

fields.name: operator_bps_fee
docs: bps legs, applied to the stake — these do NOT change with the wallet count.

fields.name: flat_fee_total
docs: Flat legs ALREADY MULTIPLIED by `shard_count`. This is what the user actually pays.

fields.name: cost_per_round
docs: Stake + both fee legs. The exact figure the deploy path will charge.

fields.name: auto_reload
docs: The behavior-shaping settings, so a position's run/recycle state is event-datable.
The full settings are always readable from the live `Deployer` account; these are the
two whose CHANGES most alter what the crank does next.

fields.name: btc_share_bps
docs: Fixed jackpot share, in bps; 0 = the overflow default. See `Deployer::btc_share_bps`.

types.name: WkDeposited
docs: USDC moved into a shard, and the stake budget that bought.
Emitted because `stake_allowance` is otherwise invisible: it is the only thing that makes
`auto_reload = false` enforceable, and a user who cannot see their remaining budget cannot
tell "my run finished as I asked" from "something is broken". Reported as the running total
after this deposit, so a fan-out across N wallets shows the budget climbing to the whole
amount rather than N separate slices.

fields.name: stake_allowance
docs: The user's TOTAL remaining stake budget after this deposit — per user, not per shard.

types.name: WkEpochRewardDistributed
docs: Sat Rush v2 no longer pays an epoch prize straight to authority-owned ATAs. Its
`distribute_epoch_reward` credits the winner's Miner/vault balances, which are collected by
the ordinary USD/sats/token claim paths. These are measured account deltas, not estimates.

types.name: WkFlagsSet
docs: Flags moved — pauses live here, so this is the event that dates every halt and resume.

types.name: WkKeySet
docs: A named address moved (fee collector, mints, the Sat Rush target...). `which` is the
`ConfigKey` discriminant.

types.name: WkManagerCreated
docs: A position came into existence. Carries `authority` — the OWNING WALLET — which no other
event does (they all identify users by manager PDA): without this, the manager→wallet
mapping was not event-derivable at all.

types.name: WkManagerTransferred
docs: Control of a whole position — funds, withdrawal rights, everything — moved to a new key.

types.name: WkParamSet
docs: A numeric knob moved. Old and new both carried so a fee/threshold history needs no
state reconstruction — the delta IS the record.

types.name: WkRewardClaimed
docs: A vault prize landed in the user's shard.

fields.name: usd_amount
docs: MEASURED across the CPI, not derived. Sat Rush computes the prize; we read the shard's
ATA before and after and record the difference. Without these two fields the largest
money event in the system — an epoch prize, or a whole bitcoin — left no on-chain record
of how much actually landed, and no amount could be reconciled after the fact.

types.name: WkSettled
docs: A deployment was settled.
Settling is what credits hashrate, and hashrate is the entire profit of this system — every
vault ticket is bought with it. It produced NO on-chain record of any kind until now, which
meant the one step between "we spent the user's money" and "the user has something to show
for it" was the only step with nothing to reconcile against.

fields.name: operator
docs: Who settled. Settle is owner-signed through our PDA, so this is the operator that ran it.

fields.name: hashrate_gained
docs: MEASURED across the CPI: the Miner's hashrate before and after. This is the number the
whole strategy turns on, and it was previously observable only by polling the account.

fields.name: rent_to_user
docs: Where Sat Rush's rent refund went. Config decides it, not the crank, and it is worth
recording per settle so a change of policy is visible in history rather than inferred.

types.name: WkShardClosed
docs: A dormant shard's two ATAs were closed and their rent returned to the user. `Manager` and
`Deployer` are deliberately left alive so the shard can still sign for a late prize — see
`handle_close_shard`.
Carries no lamport figure. Anchor closes the ATAs and credits the user directly, and the
shard's own SOL float is deliberately never swept, so the only number this could report was
a hardcoded 0.

types.name: WkTicketClosed
docs: A spent 1 BTC ticket was closed and its rent returned to the shard that paid it. Only ever
emitted for a settled iteration and never for the winning block — see
`handle_close_one_btc_tickets_batch`.

fields.name: lamports_returned
docs: MEASURED. Rent reclaim is the entire purpose of this instruction — without this field
the one path whose only product is recovered SOL reported no quantity at all.
(`WkShardClosed` deliberately carries no lamport figure; this is the one place a real
number exists to report.)

fields.name: tickets
docs: How many tickets the closed block held, for reconciling against the buy events.

fields.name: vault
docs: `VAULT_EPOCH` or `VAULT_ONE_BTC`.

fields.name: operator
docs: Who spent this user's hashrate. `WkDeployed` carries the same field so a multi-operator
world can attribute activity; a path that SPENDS hashrate needs it at least as much.

fields.name: page_index
docs: Epoch only. Which page the entry landed on — needed to reconcile entries against pages,
and to tell a real page mismatch from ordinary mid-batch drift. u16 to match Sat Rush's
own type (`select_epoch_winner(pageIndex: u16)`), not widened for convenience.

fields.name: ticket
docs: 1 BTC only, and the single most recovery-critical field in this program.
A 1 BTC ticket is a freshly generated KEYPAIR, deliberately not a PDA, so its address
cannot be re-derived from anything. If the crank's database is lost, the only way to
find our tickets again is to scan every account the program owns. Putting the address in
an event makes it recoverable from transaction history instead — which is the difference
between "rebuild the index" and "a whole bitcoin we cannot prove we hold".

fields.name: start_ticket_id
docs: 1 BTC only. One account holds a whole BLOCK of tickets, and winning is decided by
`start <= winning < start + count`. Without the start on chain, a rebuilt index cannot
decide whether a block won without re-reading an account that may already be closed.

types.name: WkTicketsSkipped
docs: Emitted when we bought a user no tickets, and why.
It used to carry no reason, so "the knee is full, by design" and "the crank handed us the
wrong page" produced byte-identical events and a post-mortem could not tell them apart.

fields.name: available_tickets
docs: Floored to whole tickets by `/100`, so a user at 99 units reports 0 here and looks
identical to a user at 0. `available_units` below is the raw figure.

fields.name: reason
docs: A `SkipCause` discriminant.

fields.name: fault
docs: `reason >= FIRST_FAULT`.

fields.name: iteration_id
docs: Which iteration this decision belonged to. `WkTicketsBought` has always carried it;
without it here, a skip cannot be attributed to the iteration whose cap caused it.

fields.name: available_units
docs: Raw hashrate units, unfloored — the number the threshold is actually compared against.

types.name: WkTokenClaimed
docs: A Sat Rush v2 token-share claim landed in a user's shard. This is deliberately a new event
rather than extending `WkClaimed`: changing an existing Anchor event's payload would make
historical log decoders misread it.

fields.name: kind
docs: 0 = direct `claim_token`; 1 = RUSH coupled into Sat Rush v2 `claim_sats`.

fields.name: token_shares
docs: Token-vault shares requested/burned. Shares are not RUSH base units.

fields.name: token_amount
docs: RUSH base units measured in the shard ATA across the CPI.

fields.name: btc_amount
docs: cbBTC base units measured across the same CPI. `claim_token` may settle both legs.

fields.name: released_hashrate
docs: Locked hashrate released, measured from the Miner rather than estimated.

types.name: WkUserFlagsSet
docs: A user moved one of their own position switches — see `state::user_flag`.
Mirrors `WkFlagsSet` one level down, and exists for the same reason stated at the top of
this section: an indexer must be able to reconstruct a position's complete history from
events alone. Without it, a position that stops mining because its owner pressed pause
would be indistinguishable from one that stopped because something broke — the skip events
say what happened every round, but only this says when and by whom the decision was made.

fields.name: mask
docs: Which bits the write was allowed to touch, and what it set them to. Both carried so a
reader can tell "the user turned the hold ON" from "the user re-saved every switch".

types.name: WkWithdrawn
docs: Money OUT — the mirror of `WkDeposited`. Emitted by both withdraw paths; `mint` is a field
because `withdraw_tokens` is mint-agnostic (it is how cbBTC leaves).

fields.name: remaining
docs: What the shard's ATA still holds after this withdrawal, for reconciliation.
